claims.text: Known seizure disorder, unchanged exam: little testing beyond antiseizure drug levels.
claims.quote: If patients have a known seizure disorder and examination results are normal or unchanged, little testing is required except for blood levels of antiseizure medications.

claims.text: New-onset seizure or a newly abnormal exam: neuroimaging, plus electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, calcium, magnesium, phosphate and liver tests.
claims.quote: If seizures are new-onset or if examination results are abnormal for the first time, neuroimaging is required. Patients with new-onset seizures or atypical manifestations also require laboratory testing, including blood tests (serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen [BUN], creatinine, glucose, calcium, magnesium, and phosphate levels), and liver function tests.

claims.text: Head CT (sometimes MRI) is usually done right away to exclude a mass or hemorrhage.
claims.quote: Neuroimaging (typically head CT, but sometimes MRI) is usually done immediately to exclude a mass or hemorrhage.

claims.text: Follow-up MRI when CT is negative.
claims.quote: Follow-up MRI is recommended when CT is negative.

claims.text: Possible meningitis or CNS infection with normal imaging: lumbar puncture.
claims.quote: Meningitis or CNS infection with normal neuroimaging results: Lumbar puncture is required.

claims.text: Drug screens may be done, but positive results don't show causality and can be inaccurate.
claims.quote: Unreported use of illicit drugs that can cause or contribute to seizures: Drug screens may be done, although this practice is controversial because positive results do not indicate causality and test results can be inaccurate.

claims.text: Syncope mimicking seizure: ECG for an unsuspected arrhythmia.
claims.quote: Syncope mimicking seizure (eg, with myoclonic jerks): ECG may detect unsuspected cardiac arrhythmias.

claims.text: EEG is critical for diagnosing epileptic seizures.
claims.quote: Electroencephalography (EEG) is critical in the diagnosis of epileptic seizures

claims.text: A normal EEG doesn't exclude epilepsy; the diagnosis is clinical.
claims.quote: However, a normal EEG cannot exclude the diagnosis of epileptic seizures, which must be made clinically.
